Quick Read

FFLG edges VUG over one year (17% vs 15%) but badly lags over five years (60% vs 84%), keeping active management's value unproven.

NVIDIA and Alphabet together hold nearly 30% of FFLG, so a stumble at either stock hits holders harder than any diversified growth index.

Read More: Avoid these 13 retirement mistakes before they derail your future (sponsor)

The Fidelity Fundamental Large Cap Growth ETF (CBOE:FFLG) has gained 14.29% in 2026 through September 24. That puts FFLG ahead of the passive Vanguard Growth ETF (NYSEARCA:VUG), up 12.02%, but behind Invesco QQQ (NASDAQ:QQQ), up 21.27%. The latest filing shows FFLG running a concentrated book tilted heavily toward AI chips and search, so holders own a direct view on AI infrastructure spending.

Rawpixel.com / Shutterstock.com
What FFLG Owns and How It Has Performed

FFLG is actively managed: Fidelity's analysts pick stocks through fundamental research instead of copying an index. Its trading history dates to February 4, 2021, so this is an established fund with a multiyear record. Net assets were about $590 million as of July 31, 2026.

Over one year, FFLG returned 17.29% versus 14.83% for VUG. That is the case for the active mandate: recent stock selection beat the broad growth index. The case against sits in the five-year numbers. FFLG gained 59.73%, trailing VUG at 84.17% and QQQ at 99.55%. Active management has to prove the recent edge is repeatable.

Concentration drives both outcomes. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) made up 16.24% of net assets, and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) held 12.56% in one share class plus 1.03% in another. For investors, a stumble at either company would hit this fund harder than a diversified growth index.

AI Capital Spending Is the Macro Factor That Moves This Fund

Beyond NVIDIA, the portfolio holds a long list of semiconductor, memory, storage and networking suppliers whose revenue depends on data center buildouts. The single biggest macro variable for FFLG over the next 12 months is whether the largest cloud spenders keep raising capital expenditure budgets.

title: VGT vs. QQQ: Where Should You Invest $1,000 Right Now for Maximum Long-Term Growth?

VGT vs. QQQ: Where Should You Invest $1,000 Right Now for Maximum Long-Term Growth?
Stefon Walters, The Motley Fool

NVDA

Trading disclosure

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEMKT: VGT) and the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ: QQQ) are two of the more popular ETFs on the market right now, and their performance over the past decade is a prime reason why. In that time, they've averaged over 23% and 20% annual returns, respectively.

Both ETFs are equipped to continue producing market-beating returns, but if I had to choose between the two and invest $1,000 right now, I would choose QQQ.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
The difference between VGT and QQQ

Investing in either VGT or QQQ means betting on the tech sector. The difference is how much you're forced to lean on them.

VGT is as much of a pure-play tech ETF as you'll find. It holds 318 tech companies, covering everything from semiconductors to software to hardware and everything in between. QQQ mirrors the Nasdaq-100, an index that tracks the largest 100 nonfinancial stocks trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange.

While VGT is 100% tech stocks, QQQ is 66.4% tech stocks. However, they share five companies in their top 10 holdings:

Data sources: Vanguard and Invesco. VGT percentages as of Aug. 31; QQQ percentages as of Sept. 18.

The most noticeable thing is just how top-heavy VGT is, with Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft accounting for over 45% of the ETF. QQQ isn't necessarily the poster child for diversification, but it spreads its risk much more evenly across the board.

Why I would go with QQQ long term

VGT has outperformed QQQ in recent years, but the one reason I'd prefer QQQ long-term is its (relative) diversification and the few key companies VGT doesn't include.

High concentration works well when it works well. When it doesn't, it can be brutal. If I'm trying to maximize long-term growth, I want exposure to some nontech sectors, even if it's a relatively small amount. QQQ provides that, with companies in the following sectors:

Consumer Discretionary: 16.65%

Telecommunications: 4.72%

Healthcare: 4.01%

Industrials: 3.22%

Consumer Staples: 2.13%

Basic Materials: 1.25%

Utilities: 1.14%

Energy: 0.53%

As for the key companies VGT is missing, it comes down to classification. Companies like Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms are technically in nontech sectors, so VGT excludes them because it only holds companies in the information technology (tech) sector. I'd want to own all three for the long haul, especially if I'm choosing a tech-leaning ETF.

Neocloud stocks, the specialized providers that build and run data centers packed with graphics processing units (GPUs) for artificial intelligence work, are under pressure, and IREN Limited (NASDAQ:IREN) stock is falling hardest. IREN shares are down 4% to $44.09 this morning, even as the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is up 0.3%.

gorodenkoff / iStock via Getty Images

Meanwhile, CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock is falling 3% to $87.18, a softer decline than IREN's. Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) stock is slipping 2% to $238.08, the smallest drop of the three.

That mix points to selling spread across the whole group. Large-cap tech is higher while every name in this neocloud trio is lower, so IREN's larger drop sits inside a wider retreat for GPU cloud providers. The question for IREN is how much of its decline belongs to the group and how much reflects the research notes that stacked up earlier in the week.

Redburn's Neutral on IREN Was Its Friendliest Call

Those notes date to September 23, when Rothschild & Co Redburn initiated coverage of the neoclouds and SemiAnalysis published the latest edition of its ClusterMAX GPU cloud rating system. Redburn analyst Alex Haissl started IREN at Neutral. He set a $40 price target, writing, "We initiate coverage of IREN at Neutral, as its unit economics and the risks of converting its business plan are fairly priced."

Potential upside for IREN, in Redburn's view, would come from additional large-scale tenant agreements and better execution at existing sites. Tenant demand, financing costs and construction disruption make up the downside list, and each one ties directly to how quickly new capacity can come online.

Friday, September 25th, 2026

In a big blow for advocates of lowering interest rates, bond yields continue to escalate in Friday's pre-market. We normally don't talk about the 30-year bond yield, but this has risen to 20+ year highs this morning: +5.480%. The 10-year yield is now +5.188% and the 2-year is up to +4.906%. These numbers are telling us that there are investment options beyond the equities market, presently.

Pre-market futures are in the green at this hour — +111 points on the Dow, +110 on the Nasdaq and +17 points on the S&P 500. The small-cap Russell 2000 is up +4 points on the final trading day of the week. This may have to do with lower oil prices overnight: $92 per barrel (/bbl) on WTI and $104/bbl on Brent crude. These are obviously still elevated levels compared to where we were earlier in this seven-months-long conflict in Iran, but perhaps enough for bullish investors to find their sea legs again.

Durable Goods Orders Outperform Expectations

The August print for Durable Goods Orders came in at 0.0%, which is unremarkable until you look at what had been expected: -0.3%. This follows an unrevised +1.1% from July. Ex-transportation, we see this figure buoy up to +0.3%, which is down from +0.7% the prior month. Non-Defense, ex-aircraft — a proxy for "normal" business spending — reached a surprisingly high +1.6%, more than triple the +0.5% analysts were expecting.

Shipments also improved month over month: -0.2% in August, from -0.9% in July. All these numbers represent an expected reversion from the prior month's rather widely dispersed Durable Goods report. And despite projections for the first negative headline since May, this big-ticket-order metric shows the American economy on firm footing.

What to Expect from the Stock Market Today and Next Week

After the opening bell, the final read on the University of Michigan Consumer Survey hits the tape. The preliminary report showed a dire 47.8, down from 51.7 the prior month. This is the lowest print since May's all-time-low 44.8, as personal finances project weaker and business finances, while steady, are well below historic levels.

This report does not use the 50 level as a demarcation point between growth and loss. Rather, it is normalized against a baseline of 100, which means we are well off norms in terms of consumer outlook. Even our near-term high — July's 55.2 — is on the low end of this well-regarded consumer survey.

Next week is "Jobs Week," where JOLTS for August happen Tuesday, private-sector payrolls from ADP ADP are Wednesday, Weekly Jobless Claims are on their normal Thursday morning report schedule, and Friday brings us the Big Kahuna: non-farm payrolls from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Estimates currently vary pretty widely: while +162K new jobs are expected to have been created in September, only +38K are expected on the ADP private-sector read.
